cards.explanation: The answer is incense. Israel burned fragrant incense on the altar every morning and again at twilight (Exodus 30:7-8). David, Israel's king, asks for his prayer to be set before the LORD "like incense." A sweet-smelling smoke rising up is the picture, and it sure beats my oven smell when I forget the timer.

The answer is guarding what he says. David prays, "Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips." The door of the lips is where words walk out. I think David knows how fast a word can leave once that door swings open.

The answer is heart. David prays, "Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing…" He's asking about the inside, where the pull starts, not only about what he does. That's a prayer worth stealing, friends.

The answer is False. David says, "let me not feast on their delicacies." He wants no share in the works of men who do iniquity, and no share in their treats either. I've turned down plenty of cookies in my day, but never because of who baked them, and this isn't about that.

The answer is a righteous man. David says, "Let the righteous man strike me; let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion." He's asking for a hard word from someone good. Not many people sign up for that, and I'd probably ask for a cookie first.

The answer is a kind act of love. David prays, "let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion." He's asking for that rebuke to be an act of loving devotion, not an attack. Then he calls it "…oil for my head…" and I think that tells you how welcome it is.
The answer is True. Verse 5 ends, "For my prayer is ever against the deeds of the wicked." Notice it says the deeds, not a list of names. David prays all the time against what the wicked do.

The answer is that the people will listen to David's words. David says, "When their rulers are thrown down from the cliffs, the people will listen to my words…" So when those rulers fall, people turn their ears to him. It's a quiet room all of a sudden, and I'd love that for my kitchen.

The answer is True. David says, "…the people will listen to my words, for they are pleasant." The verse gives that reason right in the same breath. Pleasant words get listened to, and I wish my 'do not touch the cooling rack' talk were that pleasant.

The answer is someone plowing the soil. David says, "As when one plows and breaks up the soil, so our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol." Soil broken up and turned over is the picture he uses. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's meant to be.

The answer is the Lord. David says, "But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord." Even with a verse about scattered bones right before it, his eyes stay on God. That's the right place to look, friends.

The answer is leave his soul defenseless. David says, "In You I seek refuge; do not leave my soul defenseless." He runs to the LORD for refuge and asks not to be left without defense. It's a plain, honest prayer, and I like those best.

The answer is False. David asks God, "Keep me from the snares they have laid for me, and from the lures of evildoers." He wants to be kept out of the traps, not to set any himself. Then he says, "Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I pass by in safety."

The answers are nets and safety. David prays, "Let the wicked fall into their own nets…" The nets are theirs, not his. That's what he asks for the wicked. The verse ends, "…while I pass by in safety." David isn't asking for a fight. He wants to walk right on past, unharmed.
